#9683. ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI

The Android malware has expanded from focusing on cryptocurrency theft to full device control, and the attackers have added advanced analysis of stolen information.

Android cryptocurrency stealer ArcticRAT has evolved into a sophisticated remote access Trojan (RAT) capable of taking control of victim devices, harvesting sensitive information, and using AI to identify valuable financial data.

Researchers at Zimperium who are tracking the malware described it as representing a "dangerous escalation" in the mobile threat landscape. The newer versions, according to the vendor, give attackers the ability to interact with infected devices in real time, rather than relying purely on hardcoded actions.

The malware uses multiple techniques, including a "completely black, un-dismissible" screen overlay to conceal attacker activities from victims. Most significantly, the operators of ArcticRAT are now using large language model (LLM) services to automatically sift through stolen text messages and other data from infected device for financial information worth exploiting.

Related:APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

"ArcticRAT uses AI to read through user information such as SMS messages to filter for financial information that could be used perform fraud," Nico Chiaraviglio, chief scientist at Zimperium, tells Dark Reading. "One particularly challenging technique is hidden remote control combined with a black-screen overlay. Attackers abuse legitimate Android features while making the device appear locked or powered off."

Defending against threats like ArcticRAT requires organizations to deploy AI-powered, on-device threat detection, enforce controls over application installation and permissions, and use runtime application protection to identify suspicious screen-sharing activity and malicious overlays, he adds.

Early versions of ArcticRAT targeted users of 11 specific cryptocurrency applications. Its primary purpose was to harvest sensitive information from infected Android devices that attackers could use to gain access to victims' cryptocurrency accounts.

In contrast, the newer versions that Zimperium is tracking pack considerably more capabilities. These include remote device control and surveillance, credential and keystroke theft, screen capture, live screen streaming, microphone monitoring, and the theft of SMS messages, contacts, and call logs. Another feature allows attackers to steal or change device lock-screen credentials, potentially locking victims out of their devices.

Since July, Zimperium analysts have identified 78 unique malware samples, 42 dropper samples, 36 payloads, and 21 IP addresses that the malware operators have been using for command-and-control communications. The researchers also identified 129 distinct commands that attackers can use to remotely control infected devices, steal information, monitor user activity, and manipulate device functions.

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

The operators of ArcticRAT 2.0 are using malvertising, smishing, and third-party forums to direct visitors to malicious websites in which the malware is embedded, "The primary attack vector," according to Zimperium, "relied on a landing page that convincingly impersonated Google Play to trick targets into downloading a malicious application." In some instances, the researchers observed the attackers using Amazon Web Services storage buckets to deliver the payload directly on Android devices.

Once installed, the latest version of ArcticRAT — like prior versions — abuses Android Accessibility Services permissions to connect with its command-and-control (C2) servers, giving attackers remote control over the device. The malware first collects information about the compromised device, including its location, battery status, screen state, Wi-Fi connectivity, and currently active applications.

It sends the information to the cyberattackers, who can then select which functions to activate based on the victim's device and installed applications. This can include actions as varied as capturing keystrokes, taking screenshots, recording screen activity, monitoring microphone audio and extracting sensitive information from messages and applications.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

One of the more significant additions to ArcticRAT is its use of artificial intelligence to analyze information stolen from compromised devices and identify data of potential financial value. Zimperium found the malware featuring an API connection to xAI's Grok model, which attackers can activate remotely to examine the victim's installed applications and identify banking, cryptocurrency, and trading platforms.

The new AI capabilities allow ArcticRAT to process stolen SMS messages, separate routine communications and promotional messages from information such as one-time authentication codes, account balance changes, and transaction notifications. It can even estimate a victim's financial standing before sending the information to its command-and-control infrastructure, according to Zimperium.

This allows attackers to automate much of the work involved in sorting through large volumes of stolen information and identifying potentially valuable financial intelligence, rather than having to manually examine the data themselves, according to the firm. "As mobile Trojan threats like ArcticRAT become increasingly sophisticated, conventional signature-based security layers are no longer sufficient to protect enterprise mobile endpoints."

ArcticRAT's transformation from a targeted cryptocurrency stealer into a sophisticated RAT is an example of how quickly mobile threats are evolving, with attackers using AI to make their malware more capable and dangerous. Analysts have noted how the trend underscores the need for users and organizations to stop treating their mobile devices as secondary security concerns and instead apply the same level of threat monitoring, access controls and security protections as they do to traditional endpoints.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9680. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9679. As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

It's hard to detect whether someone is using artificial intelligence (AI) to cheat on IT certification exams, but new tools and processes are emerging to boost trust.

Certifications play a critical role in keeping up with the latest industry trends and changes and in establishing expertise, but artificial intelligence (AI) is now muddying the verification process and making it difficult for organizations to know that the person they hired can actually do what their certification says they can.

There are a range of available certification options, from entry-level cloud and cybersecurity knowledge to specific Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services technologies. In some industries, such as government, banking, and financial services, certified IT departments are required to stay current with compliance regulations.

From Meta Glasses to AI browsers and deepfakes, exam administrators face a growing list of risks to monitor — including the possibility that test-takers are using AI to answer exam questions — which cast doubt on the legitimacy of the scores. As a result, the industry is shifting toward more in-person testing and stricter fraud-detection protocols to keep certifications credible.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Cheating is a risk that has existed for as long as testing has. But AI has significantly changed the testing game for IT certification, explains Marielle Carlos, data forensics scientist at Caveon. The company offers test security technologies and services to help organizations design and administer tests.

Methods such as harvesting pre-knowledge, plagiarism, and collusion proxy testing have evolved as people increasingly use AI as an unauthorized aid, she says, making cheating an incredibly challenging problem. Troublingly, the problem is still in its infancy. Up until recently, the company had identified six distinct ways people could cheat on these exams, but AI is blurring the lines between these tidy buckets. It's hard to tell whether an AI agent is gathering test questions in advance or helping during the test itself. To capture emerging anomalies that seem likely related to AI, Carlos created a new seventh "unknown" tag in the company's threat-tracking taxonomy, she says.

"It makes it hard to know if your exam is measuring actual competence or if it's measuring someone's ability to use AI to answer the question," Carlos tells Dark Reading. "It really challenges the usefulness of that exam."

Carlos spends her day interpreting test results to help programs decide whether anomalies warrant any additional attention or professional review. Over the past two years, she has seen how AI has changed the way certification programs monitor metrics to assess cheating. Previously, it may have been enough to look at speed and score separately to flag a case for review. Now attention has shifted, as administrators are forced to take numerous variables into account since AI can combine multiple cheating tactics.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

During her research, Carlos noted a "huge boom of people" who are testing fast and receiving high scores. There is no concrete data indicating it's entirely due to AI, but there is enough organizational interest and concern about this growing trend that Carlos says she and her team plan to look into it further.

But uncertainty hasn't stopped other organizations from taking action. Widespread irregularities in exam results and verified cheating attempts during ISC2's online proctoring pilot exams led the nonprofit to shift to in-person testing, says Casey Marks, ISC2's chief operating officer. The consortium also implemented "the most stringent security protocols available to analyze each result and detect irregularities," including biometric and identity verification.

The testing environment mirrors the most stringent conditions used by licensed professionals, such as doctors, to provide the highest level of security available in the industry, Marks says. Regarding AI use, the fact that ISC2 offers all exams exclusively through test centers ensures that outside resources or technology are not available during exam administration, he adds.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"The candidate, the employer, and every other professional holding that credential depend on the credibility of the process," Marks tells Dark Reading.

Regardless of AI introducing new risks, certifications remain one of the most universal ways for employers to validate a candidate's necessary knowledge and skills when making hiring or promotion decisions, Marks adds.

Carlos agrees but urges programs to have conversations around protecting score validity across the entire process. A layered approach is crucial because while there are tools that can indicate possible AI use, "it's hard to pinpoint exactly," she says.

"That includes secure exam design, control during administration, analysis of results, and a clear process for responding to your security concerns," Carlos adds.

Carlos cites an experiment by Sarah Toton, director of data forensics at Caveon, comparing AI and human test-taking that found "distinct differences" in response timing. The research focused on test results and response patterns.

"When someone uses AI, they're often six to 48 times faster compared to an individual test taker," she explains. "That said, AI can get some things wrong sometimes, particularly the questions that involve some realm of human judgment."

It's ironic, but the same technology that enables people to cheat on exams is also becoming one of the most in-demand certifications employers rely on to validate real skills. Many certifications, like ISC2's Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), have evolved and continue to evolve to address the impact of AI on security best practices, Marks says. That's in addition to new AI-specific security certifications entering the market. The Computing Technology Industry Association launched SecAI+ earlier this year to help organizations secure, govern, and responsibly integrate AI into their cybersecurity operations.

"As certifications evolve, especially with AI now playing a key role in so many facets of our work, the value of certifications for employers is increasing," Marks adds.

The pressure remains on certification administrators to keep up.

InfoQ Homepage News How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development Without Overloading Developers' Machines

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read

To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel.

In fact, according to Shopify engineers, running agentic workflows in parallel quickly hogs all resources available on development machines. They explain that "three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop", on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators, and emulators. Moreover, "if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped".

Shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but, being River a Linux-based solution, it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev:

With Remote Dev, we're no longer limited by how many builds and simulators our laptops can handle. Each River session gets its own environment, so we can have one agent debugging something on Android, another working on an iOS feature, and another testing a PR, all in parallel.

Remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH. Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session.

Agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence. They can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Thanks to this setup, Remote Dev can

implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots, and create a PR. If something fails, it can inspect the logs, fix the issue, and try again, all while we focus on other tasks.

The platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes, and submit PRs. Agents can also verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes, and running the same interaction to verify the fix.

Shopify says that, after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%.

Commenting on Shopify's article, LinkedIn user Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, argued that the key advantage of Remove Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration, noting that "a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous". However, he pointed out that the article does not explain "how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once", which he identified as a key concern.

Junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern. Allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results, as "give [the agent] a red test and enough retries and it'll sometimes rewrite the test until it passes". To prevent this, he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.

Shopify says it plans to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities.

#9675. NIST Finalizes Post-Quantum Cryptography Guidance, GAO Offers a Reality Check

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The emerging technology will soon break the "lock and key" encryption currently protecting sensitive data. A new GAO report shows agencies are behind on building their defenses.

A nation-state actor breaches a network to steal medical records, classified government communications, or trade secrets, knowing full well it's encrypted and unreadable. But they don't consider inaccessibility a failure — that was actually the plan all along.

Attackers are banking on the advent of quantum computing to decode and exploit all that stolen data, now secured with traditional public- and private-key encryption. The federal government has set standards to help prepare now, but a new report warns that agencies are still not even close to implementing those defenses.

"Harvest now, decrypt later" (HNDL), a term coined over a decade ago, refers to attackers sitting on stolen data and waiting for quantum computing to catch up. Once they're equipped to decrypt it, they may sell it on the Dark Web, use it in extortion threats, or exploit it for espionage purposes. That time is closer than it appears.

Related:Nvidia Launches AI Agent Safety Platform to Prevent Rogue Activities

Threat actors are getting ready, but US federal agencies are lagging. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) laid out a technical road map to guide organizations through the process in its recent "Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards" report. Technology providers, standards organizations, and infrastructure operations on which federal systems depend are also required to meet the report's deadlines.

The deadlines to implement measures to mitigate quantum risks are set for Dec. 31, 2030, but a report by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) cautions that federal agencies are not prepared to meet them.

When quantum computing does take off, it will suddenly render the encryption organizations rely on today insecure. Its computing power will enable attackers to brute-force encryption keys commonly used to protect sensitive data across sectors. The technology is still out of reach for most organizations due to high costs and talent shortages, but progress toward mainstreaming it is accelerating.

NIST says preparations must begin now, even "before a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer has been built," labeling it a "pressing threat" because of threat actors' ability to harvest data now and decrypt it later.

Some executive order and memorandum deadlines for federal agencies, such as completing cryptographic inventories and designating a dedicated post-quantum cryptography (PQC) migration lead, have already passed. But a big one remains: By December 2030, agencies are expected to implement migrations that mitigate as much quantum risk as possible.

Related:Hardware Makers Implement Post-Quantum Cryptography as Security Threats Near

NIST urges organizations to "treat the migration to PQC as a current operational priority." But conducting cryptographic inventories, planning migration, and early deployments of PQC-enabled products and services may be difficult for a sector that already struggles with cybersecurity, largely due to legacy systems.

"Since sensitive data often retains its value for many years, starting the transition to post-quantum cryptography now is critical to preventing these future breaches," NIST states in the report.

Any major migration requires a delicate balance between reducing risk and minimizing operational disruptions. This is another reason NIST wants organizations to act now, since data stolen today could become readable the moment attackers gain access to sufficiently powerful quantum computing.

However, despite best efforts, a GAO report documents real-world gaps between readiness and reality, suggesting that NIST's deadlines may be tough to meet. The US watchdog does not mince words, headlining a chapter: "Agencies Have Not Fully Implemented Preparatory Practices for Addressing Quantum Cyber Threats."

That was the conclusion reached after analysts evaluated cryptographic inventories, funding assessments, and other planning documentation for each of the 24 agencies covered by the 1990 Chief Financial Officers Act. That constitutes all cabinet departments and independent agencies, including NASA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and the Social Security Administration.

Related:New Tool Traces AI Videos Back to Their Source

And sufficient progress is unlikely. Only half of the 24 agencies fully agreed with GAO's recommendations. The rest pushed back, hedged, or did not respond, according to the report.

Still, GAO stands by its recommendations, which, like NIST, include establishing processes to inventory vulnerable cryptography and securing funding for the shift to post-quantum cryptography.

If legacy systems cannot be migrated to address the new concerns — which is highly likely — they must plan to replace them instead, a process that could take even longer as the threat grows more dire.

GAO attributes the missed marks in part to a lack of cryptography expertise, noting that transitioning to post-quantum encryption requires specialized mathematical and cybersecurity skills that most agencies currently lack.

Whatever the reason, it's essential to act quickly, the auditor urges. Until the agencies address those weaknesses, their cryptography will not be able to withstand the threat quantum computers pose to their sensitive information, GAO's report concludes.

But forget quantum readiness — agencies aren't even fully prepared for today's threats, according to other GAO reports.

The agency has made over 4,400 cybersecurity recommendations, including 48 deemed a priority, since 2010. However, as of February 2026, more than 730 remain unimplemented.

"Until these shortcomings are addressed, federal and critical infrastructure IT systems will be increasingly susceptible to cyber threats," GAO states.

She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9674. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

#9673. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

This entry was posted on Wednesday 21st of October 2026 11:26 AM

i discovered this blog two months back from the idscan/Nexus story and was immediately impressed by the journalism on here. as soon as i heard about this doing the rounds elsewhere on social media my first instinct was “i wonder if krebs has written about it yet?” and lo and behold. well anyways, great work as usual, cheers

Maybe I should have kept my blog as pure HTML, perhaps with some perl, instead of going to WordPress.

Just don’t forget the cgi-perl and imagemaps.

Hugo, yes! I finally retired my old Drupal-based site last week and switched to Hugo. For my blog-like site, it’s perfect and saves cost, since it’s served as a static site.

This PHP flaw is a stark reminder of how much of the web runs on shared infrastructure — one critical bug can take government and business sites offline at once. I have been following the patching updates closely, and TrendWire has been a useful source for keeping up with the fast-moving security news around this story. Hopefully hosts patch quickly before mass exploitation ramps up, as the researchers warn.

The vulnerabilities can hardly be referred to as zero-days. They have been known to The PHP Foundation from 2024 but people decided that other bugs were more urgent.

What is fascinating is everyone covering this and sort of ignoring the Indian cert authority issue that made even Krebs hard to POST to days ago. S’okay, timezone and I eligiblegentleman’ed with my cheating billeta hart.

Thanks for the heads-up. I run a small film site on PHP and found out about this from your post, not from my host. If you’re on shared hosting, it’s worth opening a ticket and asking which PHP build they’re actually running instead of trusting the control panel: the version shown there isn’t always the one serving requests.

The scale of this issue makes proactive patch management more important than ever. I’d be interested to see how many affected websites remain unpatched in the weeks following this disclosure.

#9672. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9671. China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

Attackers used Cairn once again in autonomous attacks that targeted advanced manufacturing and defense sectors, as well as civil and human rights organizations.

China-nexus threat actors unleashed another wave of attacks using autonomous AI tools to compromise microprocessor manufacturers, US defense contractors, and other organizations.

The malicious activity, tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, is the second documented attack in which China-linked actors used the open source AI penetration-testing framework called Cairn for automation, they revealed in a blog post. In this latest campaign, attackers conducted 25 operations between August and September against at least 19 organizations, achieving "unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the targeted organizations," according to the post.

In the successful attacks, the threat actors obtained dozens of valid credentials; achieved mass exposure of personal data, exceeding 1 million records at one organization; retrieved military and government identities; created persistent administrator accounts in a production system; and modified a live industry standards-ballot document.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

Of the total organizations targeted, seven were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain, and three organizations were in US defense and defense policy. The attackers also targeted various human rights and civil society organizations.

According to Unit 42 researchers, the victims included an industry standards body, which suffered a password-spraying attack; a semiconductor company, where attackers brute-forced a production credential on a partner-integration application; a US teacher's union, which suffered an unauthenticated account-creation bypass on a content management system; and a defense policy think tank, where attackers targeted an open back-end registration endpoint on its identity platform.

The China-nexus actors also targeted content management systems through identity and configuration weaknesses at other organizations, including a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, an industrial-automation manufacturer, and an education nonprofit.

Cairn played a significant hand in the campaign, and the use of it "represents a shift in how attackers are applying AI to targeted offensive operations," according to the post.

"The attackers supplied a target and a goal, then Cairn planned, executed, and recorded results on its own," Unit 42 researchers wrote.

Cairn is AI model agnostic, and in this case, attackers weaponized it using Chinese large language models (LLMs) Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro. However, initial exposure to the organizations' networks came through many of the traditional security gaps found across industries, the researchers noted.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

"It doesn't matter much to a victim whether a human or an AI agent is behind the keyboard," Tyler Oliver, CEO and founder of threat-hunting platform Huntbase, tells Dark Reading. "A human might hand the tool a mission and walk away, or direct it step by step. Either way, the password spraying looks like password spraying."

Indeed, the vulnerabilities the attackers exploited were known, according to Unit 42, including "authentication bypasses; insecure direct object references; mass-assignment privilege escalation; weak and default credentials; exposed cloud APIs; and dated public CVEs."

As in the previous Cairn-driven attacks, the findings once again provide a look under the hood at how threat actors can weaponize the tool against organizations, a blueprint that may be used in future attacks.

Rather than manually directing every stage of an attack, operators supplied Cairn with a target and a high-level objective. The framework then developed its own plan, conducted reconnaissance, identified potential vulnerabilities, attempted exploitation, and recorded its findings.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

"An AI model drives each Cairn 'agent worker,'" according to the post. "Cairn coordinates its activities through a shared 'blackboard.' Agents read the blackboard and write their findings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject 'hints' at any time to help guide the operations if needed."

"Cairn has a shared record of what it's already learned, so it can build on earlier findings without a person reviewing every result and deciding what happens next," Rickard Carlsson, CEO of AI security firm Detectify, tells Dark Reading. Meanwhile, this ability to work with limited supervision is already showing up across multiple tools, including another AI penetration-testing framework, Artex, which is also being weaponized by attackers, he says.

Individual CL-STA-1238 operations lasted anywhere from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, according to Unit 42. Moreover, attackers could achieve simultaneous operations against multiple organizations, which reduced the dependence on human operators to manage each intrusion.

Though AI is changing the game in terms of speed, volume, and expanse of attacks, it does not change the "complexity" of attacks, which, as mentioned, often rely on known security gaps, according to Unit 42.

That's a spot of good news for defenders, because "identity hygiene, attack-surface reduction, and software patching remain effective" against attacks that use Cairn or other AI tools, according to the post.

However, there are other safeguards that organizations can put in place to defend against AI-driven attacks, too, says John Strand, owner of security consulting firm Black Hills Information Security.

"There are two things I think every organization should be doing right now," he tells Dark Reading. "First, continuous attack surface management. Organizations need to identify all the different services and systems they have exposed to the internet and start restricting access wherever possible."

The second key defense move is to start using cyber deception as much as possible by setting up "tripwires" that can detect attackers during reconnaissance and lateral movement "before they accomplish their objectives," Strand adds.

#9669. 'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models

Malware can lurk inside just 0.00001% of a neural network. How, then, can any user tell it's there?

AI models downloaded from the open Internet can be subtly poisoned with malicious payloads if attackers are careful enough.

Open-weight AI models have become seriously popular lately. Even early last year, McKinsey found that 63% of organizations used them, and 76% of survey respondents said that they expected to use them more in the coming years. They're auditable, developers like using them, and, perhaps most of all, they're cheap.

Like any other software you can download off the Internet, however, open-weight and open source AI tools carry some degree of risk. Last week, researchers described a technique they call "Lazarus," which could allow an attacker to poison a model using a near-imperceptible few of its neurons. Microsoft described it as turning a model into a "sleeper agent," capable of granting an attacker access to its user's environment.

"A model is a file almost nobody inspects, yet we download models from strangers and give them access to our code, credentials, and systems," explains Briland Hitaj, senior AI security research engineer at Confidencial, whose research into techniques like this preceded Microsoft's. "Malicious models have already turned up on Hugging Face, though so far they abuse file formats like Python's Pickle to run code when loaded. I'm not aware of anyone hiding payloads inside the weights themselves outside research, but that's where the research points."

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

Since at least 2020, researchers have been coming up with clever ways to store bad stuff inside of neural networks.

The premise behind this whole category of research is that the size and complexity of these networks provide cover for small, secret, but potentially powerful payloads. Just look at Qwen 3.8-Max: It's totally open-weight, so you can inspect it to your heart's content. But it's made of 2.4 trillion parameters, and probably around 100 million neurons. If an attacker plants a functioning payload in some of those neurons or parameters, how exactly are you going to find it?

The trick, then, isn't finding a place to hide a payload. First, it's getting that payload to function reliably amid so many moving parts; second, it's making sure it doesn't noticeably impact the normal functioning of the model; and lastly, optionally making the payload robust to fine-tuning.

Different researchers have come up with different ways to do it. In 2022, Hitaj and his colleagues came up with a technique called "MaleficNet," which repurposed an old military and, later, 2G and 3G mobile network technique called "code division multiple access" (CDMA).

Related:November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Very simply, they split malware binaries into tiny pieces and spread the pieces across the many individual weights that make up a neural network. It wouldn't look like anything but noise to a passerby, yet with a trigger mechanism and a way to decode the weights, they could recover, recombine, and execute the binary.

"The vulnerability comes from how neural networks work, not from a bug," Hitaj explains. "Models have far more parameters than they strictly need, so you can nudge millions of weights slightly, or repurpose a few neurons that rarely fire, without visibly changing the model's behavior. And since nobody can read weights the way they read code, those changes go unnoticed."

Microsoft's new technique compromises on capacity for simplicity. Where Hitaj proposed encoding an entire binary across many model parameters, Microsoft researchers propose sneaking a brief command inside of fewer than 10 neurons. Specifically, one must target "dormant" neurons — those that prove to have little effect on the overall model's functioning — late in a model's processing cycle, and thus more directly influential over its output. One encodes a payload in these neurons, arranged to fire sequentially, and configures them to stay largely inactive unless they're fed a trigger. Eventually, you get a sleeper agent.

Related:OnlyFans Copyright Takedowns Expose Compromised Websites

The target payload can be arbitrary, so long as it's small and formatted correctly. The trigger can be any particular user input to the model, or tool output, or something so simple as a date read in a user's terminal.

Luigi Vincenzo Mancini, a professor at Sapienza University of Rome and one of the co-authors of the MaleficNet paper, advises organizations to take a defense-in-depth approach to open-weight AI security, "rather than trying to find a single magical 'AI malware scanner.'"

Like any third-party software, users should download AI models from official sources. As an added measure, users can compare the models they download with a known, trusted baseline.

"Microsoft says that reliable detection of these kinds of modifications requires being able to diff the deployed weights against the original, unmodified weights," Mancini notes. "That's a powerful argument for treating model weights more like source code or binaries than like ordinary data files."

Next, users should scan their models in general for anomalies. Though as Hitaj points out, "No scan proves a model is clean, and ordinary testing rarely finds a trigger the attacker chose. So the key controls limit what a compromised model can do: give AI agents only the access they need, keep credentials and production systems out of reach, restrict network access, log what agents do, and require human approval for consequential actions. If a model turns malicious, you want it boxed in and visible."

Beyond restricting them from the outset, "Organizations should monitor for unexpected agent behaviour at the system boundary," Mancini says. Practically speaking, "a model emitting an unusual shell command, attempting an unexpected network connection, accessing credentials it normally doesn't need, or suddenly invoking a tool in an unusual context can be a much more actionable detection technique than directly inferring malicious intent from billions of model parameters."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9668. Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Large language models and other AI systems allow a growing number of ransomware groups to create convincing phishing emails and identify sensitive data quickly.

Ransomware attacks are expanding amid cybercriminals' increasing use of AI tools, but at the same time, fewer organizations are paying ransoms, according to multiple reports released this month.

Globally, organizations are seeing far more ransomware incidents, while the number of attacks targeting US companies has remained fairly steady. In the third quarter of 2026, for example, ransomware groups claimed 2,766 breaches, an increase of nearly 40% over the previous quarter, according to threat data released by cybersecurity services firm Halcyon.

Threat groups adopting AI is likely a major reason for the increase in attacks. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to create convincing social-engineering messaging, find sensitive data quickly, and assist attackers has largely driven the surge in attacks in other nations, says Cynthia Kaiser, senior vice president of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and a former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Cyber Division.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"We think AI is a big part of [the growth] because it has removed the language barrier for phishing," she says. "We're now seeing much more convincing phishing in Japanese, for example. Countries like Japan are treating this almost as a state of emergency."

Overall, the jump in claimed ransomware cases — up 31% from the first quarter and 39% from the second, according to Halcyon's report — has not necessarily resulted in more ransoms paid out.

Take the retail sector as an example: While 62% of attacks on companies succeeded in encrypting data — up from 48% in 2025 — less than a third (32%) of retailers actually paid to get the data back, nearly half of the 58% that paid in 2025, according to Sophos's "The State of Ransomware in Retail 2026" report.

Instead, a solid majority of retail firms (71%) recovered their data from backup, and most recovered within a week, Sophos found. Other sectors, such as local government and school districts, have seen declines in paying ransomware as well, says Chester Wisniewski, global field chief information security officer (CISO) at Sophos.

"None of them are paying the ransom," he says. "Whether there's extortion involved, whether data theft's involved, it kind of doesn't matter. They're largely not paying the ransom."

The number of ransomware groups claiming success took off in 2026, growing from 75 in the first quarter to 111 in the third, according to Halcyon data. While ransom amounts have continued to decline, the growth in the number of groups continues to pose a threat to companies, Sophos's Wisniewski says.

Related:Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

"There's been five or six new names I've seen in just the last few weeks, so it doesn't seem like ransomware's going away at all," he says. "But its efficacy has been declining as far as generating actual money for the crooks."

The median ransom demand has dropped to $700,000 in 2026, from $2 million in 2024, according to Sophos data.

That hasn't stopped new ransomware groups from continuing to appear. At the end of the quarter, about a third of all claimed ransomware successes came from groups that didn’t exist six months earlier, says Duy-Phuc Pham, a malware researcher at Trellix.

"At the top, The Gentlemen grew from a few dozen victims a year ago to the most active group, ahead of Qilin," he says. "That kind of success makes them the obvious next target for law enforcement, which spent this year going after the shared services these groups depend on, from criminal VPNs to laundering services."

With attackers increasingly using AI, ransomware gangs will continue to broaden their campaigns against more industries in more regions — part of the reason that Europe has witnessed an increase in attacks, while US victims' share of incidents has remained the same or decreased, says Pham. AI allows attackers to create more convincing social-engineering messaging in a variety of languages, removing a significant historical barrier to targeting smaller populations.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

Because of the greater scale that AI enables attackers to hit, ransomware threat actors are able to widen their coverage, he says.

"When a tool can scan, exploit, and move through networks with little human effort, a small crew can do the work of a large one, hit far more victims, and do it faster," Pham says. "That fits what we see on the leak sites: more groups and more newcomers."

The manufacturing sector continues to be the top target of ransomware gangs, because suppliers and partners often share the same platforms, so a single compromise can expose engineering data beyond the targeted company, says Halcyon's Kaiser.

The sector will likely continue to be the top targeted group in 2027, especially as international organizations continue to account for a greater share in the coming year, she says.

"I'd expect continued growth, especially outside the US," Kaiser says. "The big open question is whether more attacks means more money ... countries newly feeling the pain are paying much more attention, which should improve international cooperation."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).
