#9647. Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

At least 178 organizations, including several major brands, unwittingly exposed website visitors to hydra-like malware via a third-party platform.

Some of the world's most recognizable brands unwittingly became conduits for malware this week, after an attacker slipped malicious code into website testing scripts delivered by Optimizely, a platform that allows organizations to experiment with and optimize their online presence.

The attack potentially exposed visitors to sites operated by at least 178 organizations — including Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA — to malware capable of stealing payment card details, hijacking cryptocurrency transactions and delivering exploit kits for iPhones and iPads.

Many organizations use Optimizely to run website experiments, test different page designs and personalize content for visitors. To do this, Optimizely embeds scripts in customer websites that can serve different versions of a page or its content to visitors, track their interactions, and measure which versions perform best.

Related:NIST Finalizes Post-Quantum Cryptography Guidance, GAO Offers a Reality Check

The attackers appear to have exploited this mechanism to insert malicious code into a custom field called Project JavaScript, which allows Optimizely customers to run their own code across website pages.

British Web security monitoring service Report URI, among the first to detect the activity, documented the tampering but said it could not determine how the attackers gained the ability to modify customer projects. "We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain," Report URL founder Scott Helme wrote.

Report URI said it located and examined 1,611 unique Optimizely scripts. It found malicious code in 188 scripts associated with 178 organizations. The company has published a list of the affected websites on its site, grouped by industry sector.

Optimizely itself has said little about the incident so far besides acknowledging it and pinning it somewhat vaguely to a vulnerability in the platform's Experimentation account sign-up flow. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered," the company said.

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

Optimizely did not immediately respond to a Dark Reading request for information on the reported scope of the incident, the exposure window, or how a vulnerability in the account sign up flow could have given an attacker write access to customer projects.

"That’s the question every affected customer should be putting to Optimizely right now," says Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. "They need to know how a new account got write access to other tenants' projects, which project IDs were changed and when, and whether that path is fully closed."

Until Optimizely explains the authorization failure, customers can't judge whether the company's reported fix addresses the cause or just the symptom, he says.

The incident is a reminder that organizations need strict controls over third-party scripts running on their websites, Beals adds. Most organizations approve a third-party vendor script once during procurement and never revisit it later. Optimizely, for instance passed whatever review the 178 affected companies ran, and the malicious code still shipped from Optimizely’s own CDN under its own certificate.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

"The takeaway is that a vendor approval is a point-in-time decision, and the risk changes every time that vendor’s code changes," Beals says. "You can keep using these tools if you decide where they’re allowed to run."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, says incidents like these show why organizations implement a browser security feature called Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify that externally hosted files, such as JavaScript, haven't been altered before they are loaded and executed.

"The problem that we have here is that you may include a file in your website that is safe for months or even years and then, unbeknownst to you, a breach occurs within your vendor and that 'file that's been safe forever' is suddenly no longer safe," Reguly says.

SRI allows organizations to perform version pinning based on file hashes to protect against attacks like the one that went down at Optimizely. "The downside is that it requires a bit more effort and management to maintain your Web pages, which are often seen as 'set it and forget it' resources," Reguly adds.

Chris Nyhuis, CEO of Vigilant, says Optimizely demonstrates what happens when trust becomes an attack surface. "Organizations allowed a third party to deliver executable code into their customers' browsers, and that trust was exploited," he says.

The answer isn't to eliminate third-party technology but to eliminate "blind trust," Nyhuis says. "Restrict where vendor scripts execute, limit their access to sensitive data, monitor their behavior and changes, and independently validate what they're doing."

Furthermore, Optimizely also needs to explain how a flaw in an account sign-up process allowed an attacker to modify executable code belonging to 178 unrelated customers. "For that to happen, there had to be a path around customer authorization boundaries," he says. "Whether that involved broken tenant isolation, privilege escalation, an authorization flaw, or access to an overly privileged service remains to be established by the forensic investigation."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9645. Claude as a Teammate: A Practical Guide to AI-Powered Marketing Workflows

Head of Marketing at BotsCrew. We help enterprises move AI from isolated pilots into production systems.

Head of Marketing at BotsCrew. We help enterprises move AI from isolated pilots into production systems.

Head of Marketing at BotsCrew. We help enterprises move AI from isolated pilots into production systems.

Almost every marketing team already uses AI. McKinsey's State of AI 2025 survey found that 88% of organizations use AI regularly in at least one business function, yet nearly two-thirds have not begun scaling it across the enterprise.

At the start of 2026, our marketing team at BotsCrew matched that statistic exactly. Everyone used AI, each person alone: personal prompts, private chats, tricks that never left one laptop. In Q2, the whole company moved to one tool, Claude, and we started setting it up as a shared teammate instead of a personal assistant.

The time savings were real, and the numbers are below. But as head of marketing, I'd name a different result first: marketing stopped waiting on other teams. Case studies stopped waiting for engineers to find time. New pages stopped waiting in the developer queue. Research stopped waiting on an afternoon of spreadsheet exports.

Below are five marketing use cases: how each worked before, how it works now, and a prompt you can copy.

"Claude as a teammate" means Claude works inside a team's real systems under shared rules, instead of in one person's private chat. Picture a very smart new hire who has read every book but knows nothing about your company. Before they can do good work, they need three answers.

The hardest part, the instructions, Claude can draft itself. We open a new chat in Claude Cowork and send this:

I want to create a Claude Cowork project for [team or task]. Our team works according to the approach on this page [link to wiki page]. Gather information from [call recordings, Slack, and all other available sources] and write a description and instructions for the project using the template from [link to template].

A person reviews the draft, then pastes it into a new shared Project. How we rolled this out across five departments covers the same setup for sales, finance and PeopleOps.

Not every job needs the same container. This is how we choose:

Shared context and rules for one team or task

Customer-facing work, live systems, automated decisions

A build for an engineering team, not a project

How it worked before. For a B2B buyer choosing an AI vendor, a case study with real numbers is the strongest proof we can deliver. Our sales team even builds proposal decks from a bank of approved ones. Yet case studies were our slowest format. The facts lived with the project team, spread across Jira tickets, Confluence pages and client calls, and the people who knew them were busy with client work. Every case study meant interrupting engineers and PMs, then waiting. Gathering, writing and design took 1–2 weeks.

How it works now. With connectors in place, Claude gathers the facts itself. When we needed an urgent case study the flow looked like this:

The quote sorting matters more than it looks. A quote that reveals how a client runs internally can't go public. Claude flags it; a person still makes the final call.

I'm writing a case study about [project name] for our website. Using Jira, Confluence and our Fathom call recordings, gather: the client's problem, what we built, the tech stack, timeline and measurable results. Then find client quotes from calls that could work as a public testimonial. For each quote, mark whether it is safe to publish or contains confidential details, and explain why. Write the case study as challenge, approach, solution, results. Use only numbers you found in the sources and name the source for each. If a number is missing, write [missing] instead of guessing.

Before → after: 1–2 weeks → about 2 hours, including our proofreading. Nobody on the project team gets pulled into a meeting.

How it worked before. Apart from client referrals, about 90% of our new business comes in through the website. When BotsCrew repositioned around AI consulting, we needed new service and landing pages fast. The blog ran on WordPress, so marketing could publish there, but each post took 2–3 hours of fighting the platform. Every other page was custom-coded and needed a designer, then a developer. Those developers were on client projects, so our pages waited, and SEO work waited behind them.

How it works now. We rebuilt the website with Claude and split the jobs. Sanity, a headless CMS, holds the content, and marketing publishes there directly. Claude builds the front end:

The two prompts we use. In Claude Design, with the website code, the Figma file and the spec attached:

Design a new page for the BotsCrew marketing website based on the .docx spec prepared by the Marketing Department. The page should look modern and match the overall feel and styles of other pages to look consistent.

Your task is to implement a new page in the BotsCrew marketing website based on the generated prototype HTML page by converting the prototype into a proper, production-ready page.

Before → after: a custom sales page went from weeks to 2–3 hours. A blog post went from 2–3 hours to about 30 minutes. Designers and developers now review the output instead of producing it, and someone technical still checks the code and deployment before a page goes live.

How it worked before. B2B buyers increasingly skip the search results page. They ask ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity who to hire and get a short list of vendors. If we're not on that list, the buyer may never visit our site, however well we rank. AI assistants favor a clear answer they can lift, sections that make sense out of context, sourced numbers and comparison tables. Our articles started from keywords, and validating which questions to target meant an afternoon of exports and spreadsheets.

How it works now. One writer runs a four-stage process, with Claude connected to Ahrefs through MCP so it pulls search data directly. The writer makes the decisions and owns the text. The stable steps live in a skill, which is how we think about Claude marketing skills: a playbook that runs the same way every time.

Prompts from our internal guide, used in order:

I'm writing an article on [topic], aimed at [audience], at the [TOFU / MOFU / BOFU] stage. Give me 10 questions a buyer would actually type into ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity on this topic. Mix definitional, comparative, cost, and "is this right for my situation" phrasings. Write them the way a person prompts, not the way an SEO writes a keyword.

Run these 10 questions through Ahrefs. For each, give me the search volume, keyword difficulty, and the closest-matching terms and search suggestions. Then tell me which 5–8 to keep: the ones with real demand that we can answer better than a generic source. Flag any that are too competitive.

Here are the questions I'm keeping. Draft an outline where each is a self-contained section. Flag which need a comparison table, and which need our own project data to be worth citing.

Before → after: an afternoon of exports → a validated question list in minutes. One writer now covers research, drafting, review and repurposing. Our Claude for marketing guide has the full prompt set.

How it worked before. Link building is one of the slowest parts of SEO. Every mention from another site is a negotiation by email, so our link-building specialist handles dozens of emails a day with hundreds of sites. The hard part was memory: we already work with this one, that one declined, this one needs a follow-up in a month. The list lived in a Google Doc, so every reply started with Ctrl+F. A small tool would fix it, and in most companies a small tool means a ticket to engineering that never reaches the top.

How it works now. He described what he wanted in plain words, in an ordinary chat, and sent screenshots whenever something broke. Claude wrote all the code. The result is a Chrome extension that highlights domains inside Gmail: green for "already have it," red for "not a fit," yellow for "promising." To tag a new site, he selects it and picks a color from the right-click menu. The database holds 800 domains, and each status shows the moment he opens an email.

I'm not a developer. I want a Chrome extension that highlights website domains inside Gmail emails based on a list I keep. Each domain has one of three statuses: green = already working with us, red = not a fit, yellow = promising. When I select a domain in an email, I want to set its status from the right-click menu. The list should be saved in the browser so it survives a restart. Write the full code and give me step-by-step instructions for installing it in Chrome. I'll send screenshots if something doesn't work.

Before → after: 1–2 hours a day spent cross-checking a spreadsheet → zero. The status is in the email. He also says a long list of sites in one email no longer feels overwhelming.

How it worked before. On any morning, a marketer's inbox holds partner replies, ad and analytics alerts, industry newsletters and requests from colleagues. Only a few need action today, but finding them means skimming everything. Email is also only part of it: follow-ups get promised in Slack threads and action items get agreed on calls. The real cost is the reply that never got sent.

How it works now. This is our simplest use case and the easiest one to copy. A Claude Cowork scheduled task runs every weekday morning and sorts the last 24 hours of email into categories the person defined. Connect Slack, and Claude also checks who is still waiting on you and what you promised. Connect a call notes tool such as Granola, and it adds the action items you agreed on. You start the day with one list. For more ways to use Cowork beyond this, this HackerNoon collection of Cowork tips is a good companion.

Prompt you can adapt (set it to run every weekday morning):

Every weekday at 9:00, go through my Gmail from the last 24 hours and group the emails into: 1) needs my reply today, 2) worth forwarding to a colleague (suggest who), 3) AI and marketing industry news from newsletters, one line each, 4) everything else, as a count only. Then check Slack for messages from yesterday where someone is waiting for my answer or where I promised to do something. End with one combined to-do list for today. Don't reply to or send anything yourself.

Before → after: the first part of the day went to sorting the inbox → one list, ready before you open email. The last line of the prompt matters: the task reads, it never sends.

Across the five use cases, work that took weeks or hours now takes hours or minutes.

A teammate still gets reviewed. These rules sit in our project instructions:

The model breaks in four situations: a connector doesn't allow the action you need, Claude gets too little context, nobody reviews the output, or the task is really a customer-facing product. The first three have workarounds. The fourth needs a different kind of build: an assistant that answers customers from a live ERP needs architecture, integrations, response validation and security. I wrote about that jump in what it takes to make a Claude prototype enterprise-ready.

Start with one routine task your team does every week the same way: a report, a status update, a case study, a round of outreach emails. Then follow the order we use:

Anthropic's own guide to scaling workflows with Claude Cowork suggests a similar model, where a few champions build starter skills for their team.

If most answers are yes, you have a teammate job. If the last one is no, you have a build.

What does "Claude as a teammate" mean? It means Claude works inside a team's real systems under shared rules, instead of in one person's private chat. It takes three things: instructions that set Claude's role and rules, connectors that give it context from tools like Jira, Slack and Google Drive, and playbooks for recurring tasks.

How do marketing teams use Claude Cowork? Common Claude Cowork use cases for marketing are case studies drafted from project records, research and drafts for AI-search articles, website pages through Claude Design and Claude Code, small internal tools, and scheduled morning digests of email and Slack. A person reviews every output before it is published or sent.

What are Claude marketing skills? A skill is a reusable set of instructions that produces a fixed kind of output, such as a researched article outline or a monthly report. Marketing teams turn their most repeated playbooks into skills, so every run follows the same steps and rules.

Is it safe to connect Claude to HubSpot, Gmail and Slack? Official connectors give Claude controlled access to the data it needs, which is safer than pasting data into chats. On Claude Team and Enterprise plans, only organization Owners can add custom connectors. Add written rules on top: numbers only from named sources, and nothing sent until a person approves it. Connecting Claude to enterprise data goes deeper on MCP.

Can a marketing team do this without developers? Mostly, yes. Case studies, AI-search articles and the daily digest run on connectors and prompts, and the Chrome extension was built by someone who doesn't write code. Website pages are the exception: Claude Code writes the page, but someone technical should review the code and deployment before it goes live.

#9644. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9643. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

#9642. Embedded Reporting in .NET SaaS: 4 Architecture Patterns and the Pitfalls That Break Them

Thousands of development teams trust in List & Label, the multiple award-winning report generator.

Thousands of development teams trust in List & Label, the multiple award-winning report generator.

Thousands of development teams trust in List & Label, the multiple award-winning report generator.

When a SaaS team says, “Let’s add reporting,” it often means one concrete thing: add a PDF download. That framing works until per-customer layouts, tenant isolation, audit requirements, and end-of-month traffic arrive. Then reporting stops being a controller action and becomes a subsystem.

Embedded reporting is also not the same as bolting on a BI platform. BI tools are optimized for exploration across data sources. Embedded reporting sits inside your product. It consumes domain data, inherits your authorization model, generates operational documents, and has to behave like the rest of your application.

For .NET SaaS teams, the durable decisions are architectural: where rendering runs, who controls templates, how tenant context reaches the renderer, and how report jobs are isolated under load. Here are four patterns that work, the failure modes that break them, and the questions to ask before choosing an SDK.

Most implementations combine several of these patterns, but one usually dominates. The dividing lines are rendering location, template ownership, and the amount of design freedom exposed to users.

The application or a background worker renders predefined templates. Users request an invoice, audit report, or statement, but cannot modify the layout.

This is a strong fit when documents must remain controlled and reproducible. The cost is organizational: every layout change becomes an engineering or operations task, and customer-specific variants can accumulate faster than the team can maintain them.

A browser-based designer is part of the product experience. Developers define the data model, functions, repositories, permissions, and allowed operations; authorized users control layout, formatting, grouping, and presentation.

This can remove routine layout work from the engineering backlog. It also expands the attack surface. A hidden field in the UI is not an authorization rule: field access must be enforced when the report data is assembled and again when the job is rendered.

Each tenant can have its own branding, language, layout, or contractual document form.

The pattern works only when templates are treated as deployable assets: identify an owner, record a schema version, validate dependencies, keep history, and define rollback. A text-based format helps with review and automation, but a readable diff does not prove that the rendered output is correct.

Users create reports from scratch and the reporting environment becomes part of the product. This makes sense in data-heavy applications with analyst-like users.

It also creates a second product surface that needs permissions, documentation, support, compatibility guarantees, and resource controls. At this point you are operating a reporting platform inside your SaaS, not merely generating documents.

A single render has state: parameters, data snapshots, pagination, grouping, subreports, and export options.

The surrounding service should still be designed to scale without sticky sessions wherever possible. Put durable job state in a queue or store, make retries idempotent, and keep tenant context explicit. That gives you reproducible jobs without coupling a request to one long-lived web process.

Tenant isolation belongs before the renderer receives data.

Do not pass a shared connection and rely on a template filter to protect records. Resolve the tenant and user, construct an authorized data source, select an allowed template, then render. Treat template repositories, caches, generated files, logs, and download URLs as tenant-scoped resources too.

Templates depend on field names, functions, fonts, export behavior, and renderer versions.

Build a representative corpus of templates and datasets, then test it before every SDK or schema upgrade. Structural validation is useful, but the acceptance test is the output: render documents, compare key values, and use visual or PDF-aware regression checks for layouts that matter.

A one-page report tells you almost nothing about a month-end workload.

Test large groups, images, charts, subreports, wide tables, and the slowest data provider you expect to support. Measure queue time, render time, peak memory, output size, failures, and cancellation behavior. Some providers or formats may materialize data in memory, so verify behavior for your actual pipeline rather than assuming that every export streams.

PDF/A, accessible PDF, electronic invoicing, signatures, retention, and reproducibility are not interchangeable checkboxes.

They affect the export engine, document metadata, attachments, input data, and sometimes the entire workflow. Confirm the exact standard, profile, product edition, and version. “Supports PDF” is not evidence that the pipeline supports your compliance target.

Rendering is sensitive to fonts, locale data, image libraries, and native packages.

A report that is stable on a developer laptop can wrap differently or fail in a minimal Linux image. Bake fonts and required native libraries into the image, pin the image, and render golden documents in CI using the same image you deploy.

Feature lists are less useful than verifiable operational answers. During a proof of concept, require evidence for the following:

List & Label supports these architectural patterns through two complementary approaches within the same reporting ecosystem.

For SaaS products in which browser-based report design and interactive viewing are part of the user experience, the Web Report Designer and Web Report Viewer can be embedded into ASP.NET applications. Developers retain control over the available data, repository configuration, and surrounding application logic, while authorized users can work with reports inside the product.

For server-side and cloud-native workloads, List & Label Cross Platform provides a reporting engine for Linux, macOS, Windows, and container environments. It uses JSON-based project files and a SkiaSharp-based rendering pipeline designed for automated report generation in backend services, background jobs, microservices, and CI/CD workflows.

These approaches can also complement each other. Teams can create or edit templates with the List & Label Designer, restrict the available design features to those supported by Cross Platform, and then render the resulting reports with LLCP. Alternatively, applications can create and modify report projects programmatically through the Cross Platform object model.

This gives SaaS teams a practical choice: an interaction-focused reporting workflow with embedded design and viewing, a service-focused architecture for automated and horizontally scalable report generation, or a combination of both.

The deployment documentation includes practical guidance for running LLCP in Docker and Azure App Service as well as Docker and AWS ECS/Fargate. The Cross Platform overview and object model documentation provide the technical starting points for evaluating these workflows.

The broader architectural lesson remains the same: choose the reporting workflow that matches your product experience, deployment model, and operational requirements. A good reporting SDK should give you enough flexibility to make that choice deliberately instead of forcing every workload into the same runtime model

Embedded reporting becomes expensive when a team mistakes document generation for the whole problem. The real system includes authorization, templates, data snapshots, rendering, delivery, observability, and compatibility over time.

Pick the pattern that matches how much control your users need. Keep tenant enforcement outside the template. Treat templates as versioned application assets. Test the documents and the workload, not just the API call. Then choose an SDK whose runtime, designer model, export limits, and license fit that architecture.

When those decisions are explicit, reporting can become a dependable part of the product. When they are deferred, the PDF button is often the first line of a much larger rewrite.

Evaluating embedded reporting for a .NET SaaS product? Compare List & Label Classic and Cross Platform against your designer, deployment, and compliance requirements before choosing an edition.

#9641. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!
